fuller.text: This short essay by Paul Graham asks why talk about politics and religion goes so badly. He notes that any mention of religion on an online forum tends to turn into a fight, while topics like Javascript or baking do not. The essay argues from everyday observation, not from studies or data.

fuller.text: His first clue is that people feel they need no expertise to hold views on religion or politics, only strong beliefs. He tests one explanation: these topics have no definite answers, so no one can be proven wrong. He rejects it, because political questions with clear answers, like what a policy will cost, end in the same fights.

fuller.text: His answer is identity: the sense of who you are, built from the groups and beliefs you call your own. People cannot argue usefully about something that is part of their identity, since they are already on a side. What triggers this depends on the people, not the topic: a Bronze Age battle stirs no one, but a battle involving their own country does. So a topic that sparks fights, like comparing programming languages, may still have real answers.

fuller.text: Graham says that if this theory is right, it shows how to think better, not just which talks to avoid. His conclusion is to let as few things into your identity as possible, since more labels make you dumber. He allows one possible exception: calling yourself a scientist, which commits you only to following the evidence.

brief.text: This short essay by Paul Graham asks why talks about politics and religion so often go nowhere. His answer is that these topics become part of people's identity, meaning who they feel they are. People can't argue usefully about something that feels like part of themselves.
